content: Saline, also known as saline solution, is a sterile mixture of sodium chloride (commonly referred to as salt) dissolved in water. It is widely utilized in medical practice for various purposes, including intravenous infusions, rinsing contact lenses, and nasal irrigation. Saline solutions are available in different formulations tailored to specific applications. Beyond clinical use, saline is also employed in cell biology, molecular biology, and biochemistry experiments. The concentration of saline solutions can vary, ranging from low to normal to high concentrations. High-concentration saline solutions are rarely used in medicine but are more commonly applied in molecular biology. Normal saline (NS), which contains 0.9% weight/volume (w/v) sodium chloride, equating to approximately 300 mOsm/L, is frequently administered intravenously to patients who are unable to consume fluids orally and are experiencing severe dehydration. It is often the first-choice fluid in cases of critical dehydration that threaten adequate blood circulation, as it is safe to administer rapidly in large volumes. Physiological saline is prepared by dissolving 9 grams of sodium chloride in 1 liter of water. Given the molecular weight of sodium chloride (approximately 58 g/mole), this results in a molarity of 0.154 moles per liter. Since sodium chloride dissociates into two ions—sodium (Na⁺) and chloride (Cl⁻)—a 1 molar solution of sodium chloride is equivalent to 2 osmolar. Normal saline contains 154 milliequivalents per liter (mEq/L) of both sodium and chloride ions. Although normal saline is often described as isotonic with blood in clinical contexts, this is technically inaccurate, as it has a slightly higher solute concentration compared to blood. Other saline concentrations, such as 0.45% saline (half-normal saline) or 0.18% saline, are sometimes used for maintenance fluid replacement. These solutions often include 5% dextrose to maintain safe osmolality while providing reduced sodium chloride content. The addition of dextrose compensates for the lower sodium concentration, as its higher molecular weight ensures the solution remains isotonic. In medicine, saline solutions with added ingredients are also commonly used. Examples include Lactated Ringer's solution and Acetated Ringer's solution. In cell biology, additional specialized saline solutions are utilized, such as phosphate-buffered saline (PBS), TRIS-buffered saline (TBS), Hank's balanced salt solution (HBSS), Earle's balanced salt solution (EBSS), standard saline citrate (SSC), and HEPES-buffered saline (HBS). These formulations are tailored for specific experimental or clinical needs. Historically, saline is believed to have been developed during the cholera pandemic that swept across Europe in 1831. The use of 0.9% saline, often referred to as normal saline, appears to have limited scientific or historical justification for its routine use, aside from Hamburger's in vitro studies on red blood cell lysis.
